title: D'où viens-tu ?
subtitle: Venir, where you're from, and -er verbs

grammars.title: The verb venir

teach.title: Venir: to come
teach.body: Venir is irregular. In the singular, the endings are -s, -s, -t, and all three sound the same: “vyan”. The plurals end in -ons, -ez, -ent like most verbs.
teach.trick: Je viens, tu viens, il vient all sound like “vyan”. Ils viennent has a double n and an open “vyen”.

teach.title: Where are you from?
teach.body: Use venir de to ask or say where someone is from. Before a vowel, de becomes d': d'où = from where. Devenir (to become) and revenir (to come back) work like venir.

examples.fr: Moi, je viens de Kansas City.
examples.pr: MWAH, zhuh VYAN duh kahn-ZAHS see-TEE
examples.fa: موا، ژُ ویَن دُ کانزاس سیتی

teach.trick: D'où = de + où: from where. D'où viens-tu ? = Where are you from?

teach.title: Which country? Which city?
teach.body: To ask for a specific country or city, use De quel pays … ? (pays is masculine) or De quelle ville … ? (ville is feminine).

examples.fr: De quel pays vient Julien Leroux ?
examples.en: What country does Julien Leroux come from?
examples.pr: duh kel pay-EE vyan zhü-LYAN luh-ROO
examples.fa: دُ کِل پِئی ویَن ژولیَن لُرو

examples.fr: De quelle ville viennent les Lasalle ?
examples.en: What city do the Lasalles come from?
examples.pr: duh kel VEEL vyen lay lah-SAHL
examples.fa: دُ کِل ویل ویِن لِ لاسال

teach.title: De, du or des?
teach.body: With cities and most countries ending in -e (feminine), use de: de Paris, de France. With masculine countries, use du: du Canada, du Japon. With plural countries, use des: des États-Unis. Before a vowel, de becomes d': d'Algérie, d'Espagne.
teach.trick: Ends in -e? Use de: de France, de Belgique. Otherwise du: du Canada. Plural: des États-Unis.

teach.sub: Where are you from? Countries with de, du, des. Tap each one to hear it.

notes: venir: je viens, tu viens, il/elle/on vient, nous venons, vous venez, ils/elles viennent.
Singular endings -s, -s, -t all sound like “vyan”. Ils viennent sounds like “vyen”.
D'où viens-tu ? Je viens de Toronto.
De quel pays … ? (masculine) De quelle ville … ? (feminine)
de + city or feminine country (de France), du + masculine country (du Canada), des + plural (des États-Unis), d' before a vowel (d'Algérie).
devenir (to become) and revenir (to come back) are conjugated like venir.

drills.why: With il / elle: vient (with a t).

drills.text: Say it in French: Where are you from? (use tu)

drills.en: I come back home at six.
drills.why: Revenir works like venir: je reviens.

drills.en: What city do the Lasalles come from?

drills.text: Say it in French: I'm from Canada.

tricks.venir: Je viens, tu viens, il vient all sound like “vyan”. Only nous venons, vous venez, ils viennent sound different.
tricks.quel: Quel for masculine words (pays), quelle for feminine words (ville).
tricks.de: Ends in -e? de France. Masculine? du Canada. Plural? des États-Unis.

grammars.title: Present tense of -er verbs

teach.title: Regular -er verbs
teach.body: Most verbs ending in -er work exactly like aimer (the only exception is aller). Drop -er, then add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. The forms in the L-shape all sound the same because their endings are silent.
teach.trick: Drop -er, add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Only -ons and -ez are heard.

teach.title: Verbs that start with a vowel or h
teach.body: With habiter (the h is silent) and étudier, je becomes j', and the s of nous, vous, ils, elles links with a z sound.

examples.en: I study / I am studying / I do study

teach.trick: Vowel or silent h? Je becomes j', and you link with a z: nous_habitons, ils_habitent.

teach.title: One French tense, three English ones
teach.body: The French present tense covers three English forms. There's no separate “am -ing” in French.

examples.fr: Denise travaille à la bibliothèque ce soir.
examples.en: Denise is working at the library tonight.
examples.pr: duh-NEEZ trah-VAI ah lah bee-blee-oh-TEK suh SWAR
examples.fa: دُنیز ترَوای آ لا بیبلیُتِک سُ سوآر

examples.fr: Denise travaille à la bibliothèque tous les samedis.
examples.en: Denise works at the library every Saturday.
examples.pr: duh-NEEZ trah-VAI ah lah bee-blee-oh-TEK too lay sahm-DEE
examples.fa: دُنیز ترَوای آ لا بیبلیُتِک تو لِ سامدی

examples.fr: Oui, Denise travaille quelquefois le dimanche.
examples.en: Yes, Denise does work on Sundays sometimes.
examples.pr: WEE, duh-NEEZ trah-VAI kel-kuh-FWAH luh dee-MAHNSH
examples.fa: وی، دُنیز ترَوای کِلکُفوا لُ دیمانش

teach.trick: Je travaille = I work, I'm working, I do work. One French form, three English ones.

teach.title: Small spelling changes
teach.body: A few -er verbs change spelling to keep their sound. Manger and voyager keep an e in the nous form: nous mangeons. Commencer gets a ç: nous commençons. Préférer, acheter and appeler change before the silent endings: je préfère, j'achète, je m'appelle.

examples.en: we eat (the e keeps the soft g)
we start (the ç keeps the soft c)

teach.trick: Ge and ce stay soft: mangeons, commençons. Without the e or ç they'd sound hard.

notes: -er verbs: drop -er, add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent (aller is the exception).
The L-shape (je, tu, il, ils) all sound alike: the endings are silent.
Vowel or silent h: j'habite, j'étudie, and liaison: nous_habitons, ils_habitent.
Je travaille = I work, I'm working, I do work.
Spelling changes: nous mangeons, nous voyageons, nous commençons; je préfère, j'achète, je m'appelle.

tricks.er: Drop -er, add -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent. Only -ons and -ez are heard.
tricks.vowel: Vowel or silent h: je becomes j', and link with a z.
tricks.meaning: One French present = three English forms: I work, I'm working, I do work.
tricks.spell: Keep g and c soft: mangeons, voyageons, commençons.
